extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers of peer review methods, and policy-makers interested in editorial peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria used to evaluate the quality, effects, and methods of editorial peer review (e.g., outcome instruments, trial design features, review quality metrics, and manuscript-quality checklists) as described in a systematic review of peer-review research.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEM editor's routine quality rating (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome assessment instrument used in Callaham studies: the AEM editor's routine quality rating on a scale of 1 to 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary outcome in Callaham 2002 and Callaham 2002a to measure reviewer performance (mean rating change pre- and post-intervention). Implicit limitations: single-editor rating, possible low reliability and susceptibility to rater bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: van Rooyen 1999 eight-item review-quality instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: An eight-item instrument used to assess review quality (referenced as the instrument used in van Rooyen 1999).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Schroter 2004: reviewers rated three papers containing deliberate errors and assessment used the eight-item instrument. Reported outcomes included overall review-quality scores and detection of major errors; differences observed were small and not always sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10-item visual analogue scale (Ernst 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 10-item instrument with 3-point scale and two overall scores; items: relevance, hypothesis-formulation, randomisation, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size, statistics, outcome choice, follow-up, clarity, linguistic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess quality of reviews in a double-blind randomized trial testing bias against an 'unconventional' drug. Employed as a reviewer-assessment tool; study found poor inter-rater reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resch 2000 peer-review score sheet (importance + VAS accept/reject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Score sheet consisting of dichotomous questions and summary questions on importance (1 = trivial even if true, 5 = major contribution) plus a visual analogue scale recommending rejection or acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to detect bias favouring orthodox vs alternative therapies by presenting two otherwise identical manuscripts differing only by drug type. Demonstrated statistically significant bias in favour of the orthodox version. Includes approach to dichotomize rating scale for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodman 34-item checklist (7 topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist instrument with 34 items grouped into 7 topics (introduction, methods - subjects and design, results - subjects and analysis, discussion and conclusions, and general) used to assess manuscript quality pre- and post-peer review/editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Goodman 1994 to compare submitted versus 'ready for publication' versions. Authors reported low reliability of the checklist (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.12) and concluded peer review/editing improved reporting in areas readers use to judge importance and generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pierie multi-item questionnaires (25-item / 17-item)
rubrics_metrics.description: 25-item questionnaire (and 17-item version for later comparison) answered on five-point scales, used by volunteer journal readers to assess quality of submitted, accepted and published versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Pierie 1996; blinding achieved by sending identically appearing typescripts. Found significant improvements after peer review (61% of questions) and after editing (69% of questions), particularly in overall score, general medical value, style and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified 9-point Goodman scale (Arnau 2003)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified version of the 9-point Goodman scale assessing manuscript quality by sections with scores from 0 to 10; modification was necessary due to poor inter-rater agreement and cultural factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess effect of joint clinician-statistician review versus clinician-only review. Two blinded statisticians rated manuscripts; inter-rater agreement reported as 0.32. Analysis had to account for deviations such as 'co-opting' of statisticians into control arm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Day 2002 99-item methodological checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist developed from existing taxonomies: 99 items in eight categories for classification of comments made in manuscript reviews, biased toward methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare reviews by dedicated methodology/statistical reviewers versus non-specialist reviewers. Showed dedicated reviewers emphasised methodology and provided generally consistent methodology-focused comments; authors caution small sample limits generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elvik validity criteria for road safety studies (seven criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity assessed against seven criteria addressing sampling techniques, total and mean sample size, specification of accident or injury severity, study design, number of confounding factors controlled, and number of moderator variables specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in an open comparison of road safety evaluation studies published in peer-reviewed versus non-peer-reviewed journals; peer-reviewed studies scored higher on validity, particularly for university-affiliated authors. Choice of checklist criteria noted as open to debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability as an outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of agreement between pairs or multiple raters (reporting metrics such as intraclass correlation coefficient or kappa) used to evaluate instruments and effects of instruments/changes (e.g., new scales, training manuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strayhorn 1993 reported increased inter-rater reliability after introducing multi-item scales and training manuals. Goodman reported low ICC (0.12) for its checklist; Arnau reported an inter-rater agreement of 0.32 for statisticians. Inter-rater reliability is a key quality criterion and limitation of many instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomisation, allocation concealment and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear description and robust implementation of randomisation methods, allocation concealment, and reporting of randomisation procedures in studies evaluating peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review assessed each randomized study for whether randomisation process, reasons for drop-outs, and allocation concealment were described (e.g., Neuhauser 1989 poor description; McNutt 1990 tested blinding robustness; van Rooyen 1998 clear plan). Lack of description or weak concealment undermines validity and generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding success and assessor/editor/reviewer masking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of success of blinding/masking of reviewers, authors, and editors and documentation of measures and success rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many trials had difficult or incomplete blinding (e.g., van Rooyen 1998 58% concealment success; Godlee 1998 53% reviewer response rate raising bias concerns). The review emphasises the consistent difficulty of robust double blinding in peer-review research and recommends assessing and reporting blinding success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attrition, response rates and dropout analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting and consideration of drop-outs, response rates, reasons for dropping out, and analysis of potential attrition/selection bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several studies had low or differential response rates and unexplained dropouts (e.g., Schroter 2004 differential drop out; Resch 2000 low usable response rate; Callaham studies with attrition confounding interpretation). Analyses should examine differences between dropouts and included participants and report impact on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of outcome measures (detecting errors, review thoroughness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome measures that capture reviewers' ability to detect major errors, number of errors found, thoroughness of critique, and other direct measures of review effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Schroter 2004, reviewers assessed papers containing 14 deliberate errors; interventions increased identification of major errors post-training. Outcome sensitivity matters: some instruments detect small changes (statistical significance) that may be editorially insignificant or not sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training effectiveness metrics (knowledge vs behaviour, sustainability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics for training interventions including pre/post test scores (knowledge), immediate changes in review quality scores, number of major errors identified, time to review, recommendation tendencies (e.g., recommend rejection), and persistence at follow-up (e.g., 6 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schroter 2004 showed immediate post-training score improvements and more errors identified but effects were slight and not maintained at 6 months; Callaham studies showed improved post-test knowledge but no sustained improvement in actual review quality. Training studies should measure both knowledge and sustained behavioural change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript-level quality domains (readability, reporting, methodological quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes focused on manuscript improvement: readability, general reporting quality, methodological robustness, style, and applicability/relevance to clinical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodman 1994 and Pierie 1996 reported peer review/editing improved readability, reporting quality and style. Rochon 2002 compared peer-reviewed vs throwaway journals showing peer-reviewed articles scored higher on methodological/reporting quality, whereas throwaway journals scored higher on readability and reader appeal. Use domain-specific instruments (e.g., modified Goodman scale) and be mindful of differing journal purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of checklists and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklists and structured instruments as convenient editorial tools, with limited and variable evidence of effectiveness and reliability across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes that many ad hoc instruments have been developed and none are the same, making aggregation difficult; checklists are convenient but have limited reliable evidence to support their use. Instrument reliability (ICC, inter-rater agreement) and validation should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability and sample/context considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether study samples (journals, reviewers, manuscripts) and settings are representative and whether findings generalise beyond the specific journals or small specialist fields studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review repeatedly flagged limited generalisability due to small numbers of atypical journals, pioneer editors, or volunteer participants (e.g., many studies were single-journal or small specialty settings). Authors recommend large multicentre efforts to improve generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of reviewer bias (design to test bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design features to test for reviewer bias (e.g., randomized assignment of reviewers to manuscript versions that differ only in a single factor like treatment type or author identity) and appropriate outcome measures (importance scores, VAS accept/reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ernst 1999 and Resch 2000 used randomized versions of identical manuscripts to test bias against unconventional treatments; outcomes included importance scores and VAS recommendations. Such designs require adequate response rates and attention to inter-rater reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of specialist reviewers (statisticians/methodologists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating the impact of adding dedicated statistical/methodology reviewers on manuscript quality and the nature of reviewer comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnau 2003 and Day 2002 provide evidence that statistical/methodology reviewers can improve methodological aspects of manuscripts and produce distinct, consistent methodology-focused comments. Analyses must account for protocol deviations (e.g., 'co-opting' statisticians into control arms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome breadth: immediate process measures vs important long-term outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing between proximal surrogate measures (review scores, readability, error detection) and more important long-term outcomes (validity of published research, impact across journals, effects on rejected manuscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review criticises the literature for focusing on marginal surrogate indicators and editor-centred outcomes, with little attention to ultimate aims (e.g., validity of published research, fate of rejected manuscripts). Studies should align outcomes with the conceptual aims of editorial peer review.
